title: Estimation in the Interview
summary: How much precision is actually enough, and how to run the estimation phase as a fluent five minutes that sets up your design, instead of a stall that eats the interview.

slides.markdown:
Everything in this group — traffic, storage, bandwidth — is arithmetic you can do alone at a desk. Doing it live, narrated, in front of an interviewer with a clock running is a different skill, and it's the one that actually gets graded.

This topic covers the process layer: how precise to be, what order to work in, how to talk while you calculate, and how much of the interview this phase should actually consume.

The bar is **correct order of magnitude with consistent units**, not a number matching some hidden right answer. Rounding a day to 100,000 seconds, or assuming 50 million DAU instead of a precise 49.7 million, changes nothing that matters — no design decision flips on a 15-20% difference.

What actually hurts you is a **unit error**: forgetting to convert bytes to bits, mixing KB with MB, or confusing per-day with per-second. Those don't shift your answer slightly — they're off by a factor of 8, 1,000, or 86,400, and that kind of error changes which design you'd propose.

Be fast and rounded on the numbers; be careful and explicit about the units.

slides.sectionTitle: A repeatable structure: traffic -> storage -> bandwidth -> servers
slides.markdown:
Work the estimate in a fixed order, because each step feeds the next. Start with [traffic and QPS](traffic-estimation-qps) — DAU to requests to average and peak QPS — since request volume drives everything downstream. Next, [storage](storage-estimation) — record size to total, corrected for growth and overhead. Then [bandwidth](bandwidth-and-bottleneck-estimation) — QPS times payload size, in bits. Finally, translate all three into a server count, checking which resource actually binds first.

Doing this out of order means guessing a server count before you know the load, or sizing storage before you know how many users generate it.

Memorize the sequence, not the numbers — the numbers change per problem, the order doesn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the estimation flow as a checklist
slides.markdown:
![Horizontal checklist of four checked boxes — Traffic, Storage, Bandwidth, Servers — with a clock icon marked ~5 min](assets/estimation-checklist.svg)

Treat the four-step sequence from the previous slide as a literal checklist you narrate through, not a set of facts to recall. Each box is one or two sentences of assumptions plus one line of arithmetic — the whole pass should take a few minutes, not fifteen.

A checklist also protects you under pressure: if you go blank mid-interview, you know exactly which of the four boxes you're stuck on and can say so out loud.

assets.alt: Horizontal checklist of four checked boxes — Traffic, Storage, Bandwidth, Servers — with a clock icon marked ~5 min

slides.markdown:
Narrate every assumption before you use it — "let's assume 50 million daily active users" — rather than doing silent mental math and announcing only the final number. The interviewer is grading the reasoning, and a silent pause reads as uncertainty even when the arithmetic is fine.

A useful script: state the assumption, state the formula, do the arithmetic out loud in rounded numbers, state the result and its unit. For example: "50 million DAU, 20 requests each, so 1 billion requests a day; dividing by roughly 100,000 seconds gives about 10,000 requests per second, average."

If you're unsure of an assumption, say so and pick a reasonable number anyway — a stated, reasonable guess is worth far more than silence.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a strong estimate vs a hand-wavy guess — what the interviewer notices
slides.markdown:
| | Strong estimate | Hand-wavy guess |
|---|---|---|
| Assumptions | stated explicitly ("assume 50M DAU") | left implicit or skipped |
| Units | tracked and converted deliberately | mixed up (bytes/bits, day/second) |
| Sanity check | compared against a known reference point | none — number is accepted as-is |
| Pace | a few focused minutes | either rushed to a wrong answer or stalls for ten-plus minutes |

**How to decide (self-check):** if you can't point to the assumption behind a number, or haven't sanity-checked it against something you already know the scale of, you're in hand-wavy territory even if the arithmetic itself is correct.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: spending 15 minutes of a 45-minute interview on estimation
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Estimation is foundational, so I should get every number exactly right before moving on to the design."

**Why it's wrong:** a 45-minute system design interview weights the actual design and trade-off discussion far more heavily than the estimate. Spending 15-20 minutes chasing precise figures leaves too little time for the part being graded hardest, and an interviewer watching the clock will read it as a pacing problem, not thoroughness.

**Correct model:** budget roughly 5 minutes — about a tenth of the interview — for estimation. Use it to inform 2-3 concrete design decisions (single node or sharded, cache or no cache, CDN or not), then move on. The estimate is a means to the design conversation, not the deliverable.
